title: The YM2151 registers
covers: the registers of the YM2151 as Yamaha's application manual describes them, and MAME's handling of each

rows.text: A designated bit of the TEST register, whose position is garbled in the capture, resets the LFO output waveform; the process then restarts from the left edge.
TEST is a test-use signal: entering 1 in a place other than the designated bit makes the device enter test mode.
A key write carries a 3-bit channel number and a 4-bit slot: a 1 in a slot bit turns that sound source on, a 0 turns it off.
The four slot bits correspond to M1, C1, M2 and C2; the capture garbles the labels of their bit positions.
With noise enabled the 32nd slot becomes the noise slot; its envelope is not logarithmic: attack is exponential and decay a straight line.
NE takes effect when its bit, read D7 in the capture (doubtful), is 1, making the 32nd slot the noise slot.
The noise frequency is set by NFRQ, by a formula garbled in the capture, over about 3.5 kHz to 111.9 kHz.
MAME reads NFRQ as the low 5 bits of 0x0F exclusive-ORed with 0x1F.
The LFO oscillates over a wide range, selects one waveform from several, and provides frequency and amplitude modulation whose output levels can be controlled.
The LFO oscillation frequency is set with 8 bits, tabulated in a figure the capture does not carry.
MAME turns the 8-bit rate into a counter step: the low 4 bits with an implied leading 1, shifted left by the high 4 bits.
PMD and AMD data are each 7 bits, the first bit distinguishing PMD from AMD.
PMD and AMD set the frequency and amplitude modulation output level at 1/128 resolution; PMD is two's complement and AMD is binary.
A write to 0x19 stores the byte at 0x19 plus its bit 7, so with bit 7 set it lands in 0x1A.
MAME takes the PM depth from the low 7 bits of 0x1A.

rows.text: Two bits, garbled as Ds and D> in the capture, correspond to terminals CT1 and CT2.
CT1 and CT2 together make up the external control output port.
At initial clear, with the IC terminal at 0, the CT1 and CT2 terminals read level 0.
Two bits select one of four types of frequency (PM) and amplitude (AM) modulation waveform.
MAME's ym2151 reset only calls the engine's reset and makes no write to the CT1 and CT2 output lines.
The timer is two timers, a pre-set 10-bit Timer A and a pre-set 8-bit Timer B; both start and stop, and an overflow puts a flag on the data bus.
Timer A can also key on when it overflows, and the interrupt it raises must be stopped, which has its own control.
CLKA1 and CLKA2 are composed of two words of 10 bits, as the capture says.
With them, Timer A generates an overflow at the indicated period.
MAME builds the Timer A value from the 8 bits of 0x10 as the high part and the low 2 bits of 0x11.
Timer A overflows after 64*(1024-NA) cycles of the clock, written Ta in ms over the clock in kHz, 3579.545 here; the divisor is partly garbled.
CLKA2 is named in the Timer A diagram, where the capture garbles it to CLKA?.
CLKB is composed of 8 bits; Timer B overflows after Ts ms = 1024*(256-CLKB) over the clock in kHz, 3579.545 here; the divisor is garbled.
CLKB is an 8-bit datum, shown in a diagram the capture garbles.
Entering 1 in the two LOAD bits starts timer A and timer B, and entering 0 stops them.
Entering 1 in the two F RESET bits resets the flag registers that show timer A and timer B have overflowed.
The two IRQEN bits, one per timer, enable you to inhibit the flag register that records a timer overflow.
The F RESET bits act on the flag register contents that record the overflow of the two timers.
Entering 1 in the CSM bit keys on all sound source slots when Timer A overflows.
The operator reads the sine table with the phase information from the PG and multiplies it by the EG envelope; its FM-modulated signal goes to the ACC.
CON is one 3-bit datum per note that sets how its operators are connected, as drawn in a figure the capture garbles.
FL (self feedback level) is one 3-bit datum per note, controlled for all notes as in a figure.
The ACC takes the L/R control signal from the register, puts the signal into the left sequence, the right or both, and accumulates it.
The LR control divides the operator signal between the left and right sequences, or feeds both at once; the capture garbles the bit labels.
On reset MAME zeroes every register except 0x20 to 0x27, which get 0xC0, turning both outputs on.
A key code is one 7-bit datum per note.
The first 3 bits of a key code express the octave and the last 4 the note, related to intervals in a figure.
A clock of 3.579545 MHz and KC of OCT 4, NOTE 10, with KF, DT1, DT2 and PMS 0 and MUL 1, gives a sound of 440.0 Hz.
A key fraction is one 6-bit datum per note.
The 6 bits divide the 100-cent note interval into 1.6-cent segments to fix the phase information.
PMS is one 3-bit datum per note giving its phase modulation sensitivity to the LFO; the capture garbles the number of levels.
The LFO signals, 8 bits wide, are added to KC and KF to give vibrato and trembling sounds; the sensitivity value holds when the LFO output is maximal.
AMS is one 2-bit datum per note giving the EG's amplitude modulation sensitivity to the 8-bit LFA data of the LFO.
MUL is a 4-bit datum, four of which set one note, that multiplies the KC and KF phase information.
DT1 is a 3-bit datum, four of which set one note, that detunes the phase information from the frequency.
For both MUL and DT1, four data set one note.
TL is a 7-bit datum, four of which are used to set a note: the total level, in attenuation, that the EG applies.
TL controls timbre and volume, with a minimum resolution of 0.75 dB per bit weighting, shown in a figure the capture garbles.
AR is a 5-bit datum, four of which are used to set a note, that sets the attack time TA, and it is scaled by the key code.
At key on the attenuation volume diminishes and approaches 0 dB after the attack time.
KS is a 2-bit datum, four of which are used to set a note, that scales AR, D1R, D2R and RR by the key code, at four levels.
The attack, first decay, second decay and release times are set by each rate after it has been scaled.
D1R is a 5-bit datum, four of which are used to set a note, that sets the first decay time TD1, and it is scaled by the key code.
At 0 dB attenuation the EG moves by itself to first decay, reaching the first decay level.
The AMS-EN switch decides, for a particular slot, whether amplitude modulation applies to it.
AMS data is set for every channel.
DT2 is a 2-bit datum, four of which set one note, that gives a gross detuning of the phase information.
DT2 detuning is effective when generating sound effects.
D2R is a 5-bit datum, four of which are used to set a note, that sets the second decay time TD2, and it is scaled by the key code.
Once the first decay level is passed the EG moves by itself to second decay and stays there until key off.
RR is a 4-bit datum, four of which are used to set a note, that sets the release time TR, and it is scaled by the key code.
Because RR has one bit fewer than D1R or D2R, its resolution is poor.
At key off the EG starts release and the attenuation advances toward the maximum attenuation of 96 dB.
DIL is a 4-bit datum, four of which set a note: the first decay level, in 3 dB steps, at which the EG moves from first to second decay.
MAME makes a first decay level of 15 count as 31 steps: it ORs in bit 4 when the level plus one has it, then shifts left by 5.
